content: The International Quality Control Study 51 highlights several critical issues regarding the diagnosis and management of hepatitis D virus (HDV) among individuals with chronic hepatitis B virus (HBV) infection. Testing for HDV remains limited, and public health programs have not prioritized screening and diagnosis. HDV is genetically diverse, with eight genotypes distributed geographically, posing challenges for diagnostic accuracy. Currently, there are limited commercially available assays for anti-HDV detection (two ELISA and one chemiluminescent assay) and HDV RNA quantification (four commercial assays, with additional research-use-only options). All available assays are laboratory-based, making them unsuitable for decentralized, point-of-care testing. Furthermore, there are no gold-standard assays for anti-HDV or HDV RNA testing, complicating the evaluation of diagnostic accuracy, sensitivity, and specificity. Some assays have demonstrated good diagnostic performance compared to reference standards, but issues remain, particularly with detecting certain genotypes, such as HDV-1 African strains and genotypes 5–8. Protocols for HDV RNA testing vary widely, including in-house methods, and there is an opportunity to standardize processes, such as incorporating internal RNA controls. Research gaps include the need for further evaluation of diagnostic performance across different assays to establish reliability and potentially designate a gold standard for HDV screening, confirmation, and viremia quantification. Demonstrating assay performance across diverse genotypes and populations is essential to validate their use in various settings. Investigational methods, such as rapid diagnostic tests for anti-HDV, could help decentralize screening. Aligning public health priorities to emphasize HDV diagnosis could stimulate demand and development of commercial diagnostic products. Efforts to validate HDV assays across populations and genotypes, including the development of an international reference standard, could improve diagnostic reliability. A target product profile for anti-HDV and HDV RNA assays could guide clinical and operational performance standards. External quality control evaluations could further assess testing performance across laboratories and identify barriers to reliable diagnosis. HDV and HBV coinfection significantly increase the risk of liver cirrhosis and hepatocellular carcinoma compared to HBV infection alone. Accurate prevalence estimates of HDV infection are necessary to develop effective strategies for identifying coinfected individuals. Early HDV diagnosis enables better counseling, antiviral therapy, and follow-up to limit disease progression and transmission. Despite recommendations from international guidelines to test all HBsAg-positive individuals for anti-HDV, most have never been screened. Reflex testing for HDV serology could expedite access to treatment and care, particularly in settings with low HBV prevalence but high HDV prevalence. Reflex testing involves automatic anti-HDV testing for HBsAg-positive individuals and HDV RNA testing for anti-HDV-positive individuals. Reflex testing has been shown to significantly increase the uptake of HDV antibody testing among HBsAg-positive individuals, facilitating access to treatment and intensive monitoring. Incorporating reflex testing into the HBV care cascade could be particularly beneficial in settings with high HDV prevalence. However, data on reflex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) testing for HDV viremia are limited, and further research is needed to evaluate its impact on care linkage and treatment initiation. In conclusion, reflex testing for HDV serology can substantially improve testing uptake and access to care for HDV among HBsAg-positive individuals. Simplified guidelines and decentralized service delivery models are needed to promote access to diagnosis and treatment, particularly in primary care and community settings. Addressing gaps in the care continuum, especially for individuals not receiving antiviral therapy, is critical to improving outcomes and preventing liver-related deaths.
